table.title: The Reform Programme
table.caption_extra: In order to effect internal reforms in Korea, agreement was entered into between that country and Japan in August of last year. This reform programme is understood to be substantially as follows :—

rows: The Korean Financial Department to engage a Japanese as Superintendent of Korean finances in order to carry out fiscal reforms.
Japan to advance the necessary funds to Korea in order to enable her to effect financial reforms, 3,000,000 yen being lent as first instalment.
Sound currency system to be established by abolishing the present Mint and withdrawing the copper coins now in circulation.
Currency union to be established between Japan and Korea and Japanese money to be accepted as legal tender by the Koreans.
A Central Bank to be established in Korea to facilitate the collection of taxes and the handling of public money.
A model administrative system to be adopted in Kyong-kwi Province, and similar system to be adopted in other provinces when this experiment proves successful.
A certain American citizen to be engaged by the Korean Foreign Department as its Adviser in order to improve foreign intercourse.
Korea to recall her Ministers and Consuls stationed abroad when she decides to place her foreign affairs and the protection of her subjects staying abroad in charge of Japan.
The Foreign Ministers to Korea to be withdrawn from Sŏul and the Foreign Consuls alone to remain on duty with the withdrawal of the Korean Ministers and Consuls from the foreign countries.
The Korean army, at present 20,000, to be reduced to 1,000 and all the garrisons in the provinces to be disbanded, one at Sŏul alone being kept.
Military arms to be made common between Japan and Korea with the object of adjusting the existing military system in the latter country.
Soothsayers, fortune-tellers, and other officials ministering to superstition to be expelled from the surroundings of the Sovereign to uphold his dignity.
All superfluous Government offices and officials to be discharged.
Government posts to be made open to all classes of the people, without regard to rank and family relation.
The practice of selling Government posts to be prohibited and the officials to be selected from among those who are competent.
Salaries of the Ministers of State and other Government officials to be increased so as to awake in them a stronger sense of responsibility.

Definite educational policy to be established, and organization of universities, middle schools, and primay schools to be modelled after that existing in Japan; also technical schools to be established in order to encourage industry.
A distinct line of demarkation to be drawn between the Court and the Government.
The present foreign Advisers to be reduced in number with the abolition and amalgamation of the Government offices.
The post of Supreme Advi er to the Korean Government to remain unfilled for the present.
Agriculture to be improved by reclaiming waste lands and developing the natural resources of the soil.

table.title: Legal Status of Women
table.caption_extra: These points of difference are enumerated in the following:—

rows: The legal restriction of age in marriage is different between men and women. According to the Civil Code of Japan, men must be above 17 years and women, 15 years.

There can be no existence of marriage without the voluntary agreement of the man and the woman when a marriage is to be contracted. If they have parents living, they must obtain their consent, unless the man has completed his 30th year and the woman her 25th. In the case of minors who have no parents alive, they must obtain the consent of their guardians and the family councils.

A woman becomes incompetent upon contracting a marriage; that is, it becomes necessary for her to obtain the permission of her husband in the conduct of important legal acts, as lending or borrowing of money, transfer of her own real estate or some valuable pieces of movable property, bringing of an action in a court of law, accepting or refusing a succession, etc.
A married couple are under legal obligation to cohabitation but the right of selecting the place of residence is invested in the husband.

A wife is supported as a matter of course by her husband in this country. There are no detailed provisions for regulating the property relations of man and wife, as there are but few cases of women's marrying with large dowries.

There are two classes of divorces; divorce by consent and divorce by judicial action. In the case of a divorce by consent, there is no partiality, as mutual consent is required to make a divorce effective. In the case of a divorce by judicial action, however, the wife is very partially dealt with, for, while the committing of adultery on the part of the wife is in itself a sufficient ground for bringing an action for divorce, in the case of the husband it is necessary that the husband guilty of adultery has been prosecuted by law upon the accusation of the husband of the woman who is party to the crime. The wife, therefore, cannot bring an action for divorce against her husband even when he keeps a concubine, resorts to houses of ill-fame, or comes into illicit relations with unmarried women or widows

A wife cannot succeed to the house in precedence to a child, if she has one; in case she is without a child, she is to be chosen an heir to the house by the father or mother of her husband or by the council. A wife may, however, become an heir to bequeathed property.

In the case of succession to a house, a male has precedence over a female when there are two or more children in the house. A girl must give place to a boy even when she is his senior. A girl, even when she is a legitimate child, must give place to a boy who is a shoshi, or a natural child recognized by the father. In the case of succession to bequeathed property, the difference of sex is not taken into consideration, a shoshi and a natural child being entitled to half the share falling to a legitimate child.

transcriber_notes: Numbered list of points of difference; item 1 on p. 308, items 2-8 on p. 309. Line-break hyphenation removed; italics (shoshi) not marked.

table.title: [Buké Hatto (Samurai Law), 1615: gist of the 13 articles]
table.caption_extra: [list] Buké Hatto (Samurai Law) ... It consisted of 13 articles the gist of them being as follows:

rows: Samurai must be well educated in general learning and versed in the arts of war
Unbridled drinking and luxuriousness are strictly prohibited
Criminals must not be aided or concealed
All treasonous bodies and murderers should be banished
No person other than the subjects of the daimyo should be allowed to live in his territory
All repairs to castles need permission of the Shogunate and the building of a new castle is strictly prohibited
If anyone detects a new castle building or a secret political organization in a neighbouring province he must report it to the Shogunate
Marriages must not be celebrated privately

All the lords are required to observe “sankin-kotai”. (According to this article the lords were divided into two groups, and each group was to come up to Yédo, the seat of the Shogunate, in April every other year, to stay there for one year and the Shogunate prepared their Yedo residences where their families were kept as hostages. These rules were somewhat loosened in later years.)
Styles of costume should be regulated according to rank and social position
Servants ought not freely to use the palanquin (the only vehicle in those days) in travel
Samurai should be instructed to live frugally
the lords should use discretion in appointment of officials

transcriber_notes: Run-in numbered list within prose; the introducing sentence begins on p. 73 (p0115). Item (9) includes the parenthetical explanation printed after it. 'sankin-kotai' is hyphenated across a line break in print ('sankin-/kotai'); 'privately' is printed with a damaged initial p.

table.title: Chronicle of Important Events

rows: The Emperor Jimmu ascended the Throne at the Kashiwara Palace, Unébiyama, Yamato province, near the present Nara.
Neighbouring clans subdued by the armies of the Imperial Princes.
The Great Shrine of Isé built by the Emperor Suinin in honour of Amatérasu-Omikami.
Clans and tribes in Kyushu and the eastern half of the Main Island subdued by the armies of the Emperor Kéiko and Prince Yamatotakéru his son.
The Emperor Séimu divided his dominion into administrative districts.
The Emperor Nintoku established the capital at Naniwa (Osaka) for the convenience of intercourse with Korea.
Japanese Office in Mimana is destroyed by Silla.
Imperial Prince Shotoku became Regent, and propagated Buddhism, building Horyuji and other temples.
The Regent Shotoku proclaimed the Constitution.
The Asuka or Empress Suiko's Period of Art history.
The custom of 'year-names' introduced, the first one being called Taika (great reformation).
Ézo (Hokkaido) subjugated by the army of Hirafu Abé.
Control over the Korean Peninsula abandoned.
The Taiho Law promulgated and the organization of the Imperial Government is fixed.
The Hakuho Period of Art history.
6. Establishment of the Capital at Nara and Compilation of a History of Japan.
The Empress Gemmyo founded Nara as her capital.
The first books of Japanese history, Nihon Shoki (Japanese Annals) and Kojiki (Antiquities) compiled.
7. Spread of Buddhism and Progress of Religious Fine Art.
Building of Todaiji temple and other provincial temples.
The Empress Kōmyo donated the treasures of the late Emperor Shomu to Todaiji temple. They are kept in the Shosoin Museum, built a little later.
Dictatorship of Dōkyo, Buddhist pope, opposed by the great loyalist Kiyomaro Waké.
The Tempyo Period of Art history.
8. Founding of Héian (Kyoto) the Capital, and troubles in the north.
The Emperor Kammu founded the new capital Héian and the Government removed there from Nara.
Revolts broke out in Ézo, finally subdued by the expedition of Tamuramaro Sakanoué.
Establishment of governmental and private schools.
The Konin period of Art history.
Mototsuné Fujiwara the Daijo Daijin and Regent became Kampaku (Chief Councillor) at the same time.
Michizané Sugawara, candidate for Kampaku reduced to the position of governor of Kyushu by the Fujiwara scandal.
Official intercourse with Tang broken off by the advice of Michizané Sugawara.
Bokkai, a maritime monarchy in Manchuria, traded with Japan.
11. Disorder in Rural Districts and Rise of the Samurai.
Masakado Taira rebelled and proclaimed himself Emperor.
Sumitomo Fujiwara disturbed the coasts of the Inland Sea but is suppressed.
The Samurai families of Minamoto (Genji) and Taira (Héishi or Héiké) gradually rose to power.
Michinaga Fujiwara assumed the Regency for the next 20 years and his son Yorimichi for 50 years. Climax of the Fujiwara despotism and prosperity.
Toi tribe in the north-eastern part of Korea invaded the islands of Iki and Tsushima.
Tadatsuné Taira's treason in Shimoosa province.
Armies of Buddhist monks rose in revolt.
The Abés in the Ohu district declared independence.
The ex-Emperor Shirakawa took part in politics for nearly 40 years and set a precedent for government by ex-Emperors.
The Ohu district again disturbed by the Kiyowaras.
For about a century the family of Kiyohira Fujiwara who subdued the Kiyowaras ruled over the Ohu district.
Strife between the armies of the Emperor and the ex-Emperor (Hogen war).
The Fujiwaras and Minamotos waged war against another branch of the Fujiwaras and the Tairas (Héiji war).
Kiyomori Taira promoted to Daijo Daijin.
Autocracy of Kiyomori and his family.
Rise of the Minamotos in rivalry to the Tairas. Yoritomo Minamoto established headquarters at Kamakura.
The Tairas destroyed by the armies of Yoshitsuné, brother of Yoritomo.
Yoritomo appointed local military police and tax-gatherers for rural districts.
The Fujiwara Period of Art history.
15. Beginning of the Kamakura Shogunate Régime.
Yoritomo Minamoto promoted to Séii-Taishogun (Generalissimo) and the Shogun Government formally sanctioned. For the next 675 years Japan ruled by the samurai statesmen.
Tokimasa Hojo became chief executive of the Shogunate régime.
Minamoto Shogunate ended with the third Shogun, Sanétomo. But Masako, widow of Yoritomo, (called the 'Ama' or Nun Shogun) officiated as Shogun for several years.
Trouble between the Kyoto Court and the Hojos (Shōkyu affair).
Yasutoki Hojo became chief executive of the Kamakura Shogunate.
The Hojos continued to exercise the Shogun's duties for over a century.
The Joéi Code promulgated for the discipline of the samurai.
Second Yuan invasion and defeat by the armies of Tokimuné Hojo, the chief executive.
An attempt for the restoration of the Imperial Rule.
War between the Imperial and the Hojo armies.
17. The Emperor Godaigo and Takauji Ashikaga.
Temporary restoration of the Imperial direct rule by the Emperor Godaigo.
Takauji Ashikaga rebelled against the Emperor.
Masashigé Kusunoki, famous loyalist, died in the battle of Minatogawa (Kobé).
The Emperor Godaigo moved to Yoshino mountain.
The Imperial House divided into two, the South and the North (Yoshino and Kyoto) for 57 years.
The Kamakura period of Art history.
18. Beginning of the Muromachi Shogunate and the luxurious age of Yoshimitsu.
Takauji Ashikaga proclaimed himself Shogun and established the Muromachi Shogunate in Kyoto.
Takauji sent the Tenryuji-buné (trade boats) to China.
Yoshimitsu Ashikaga publicly appointed Shogun and the Muromachi Shogunate officially sanctioned.
Yoshimitsu traded with Ming: indulged in luxurious living.
19. Corruption of the Muromachi Shogunate and Political Commotion.
The Éikyo Rebellion. Rising of military lords in Kanto district.
The Ohnin war: Kyoto reduced to ashes in the street fighting. The Court and the Shogunate both lost power and the whole country became a scene of warfare among the military lords.
20. A Century of Civil Wars Among the Feudal Lords.
Soun Hojo captured Odawara Castle and ruled over the Kanto district.

Feudal lords struggled for supremacy, the greater lords being as follows: Kanto district; Hojo, Uésugi. Ohu district; Daté, Ashina, Mogami, Tamba, Akita. Central district; Uésugi, Takéda, Imagawa. Kinki (Kyoto-Osaka) district; Saito, Asai, Asakura, Oda, Matsudaira. Chugoku (Western Main Island) district; Ukida, Amako, Ohuchi, Mori. Shikoku Island; Miyoshi, Kono, Chosokabé. Kyushu Island; Otomo, Ryuzoji, Shimazu.
The Muromachi Period of Art history.
Nobunaga Oda came up to Kyoto by Imperial order and repaired the Palace.
Nobunaga destroyed Énryakuji temple to suppress the power of the monks.
Hidéyoshi promoted to be Kampaku and Daijo Daijin.
Unity of the Empire realized by Hidéyoshi, all the lords completely subdued.
Invasion of Korea by armies of Toyotomi.
Hidéyoshi Toyotomi died at Fushimi castle (Momoyama Palace).
The Momoyama period of Art history.
Battle of Sékigahara assured the supremacy of Iyéyasu Tokugawa (1542-1616).
Iyéyasu appointed Shogun and founded the Yédo Shogunate.
The Loochoo Islands subjugated by Lord Shimazu.
Sending of official letters to Nova-Hispania and Spain.
Iyéyasu prohibited the preaching of the Catholic Faith.
The lord Masamuné Daté sent Hasékura to Rome.
The Toyotomis destroyed at the Battle of Osaka.
Proclamation of the Kugé Hatto (Court Nobles Law) and the Buké Hatto (Samurai Law).
Iyémitsu (1604-1651) became the third Tokugawa Shogun. Under his enlightened rule the position of the Yédo Shogunate became unshakable.
Death of Iyémitsu and attempted rebellion by Yuino Shosétsu and his colleagues.
24. The Golden Age of the Yédo Shogunate.
Mitsukuni Tokugawa, lord of Mito began the compilation of the Dai Nippon Shi (Great Nippon History).
The Shogun Tsunayoshi's Edicts for the protection of animals caused much loss of human life.
The Genroku Era of luxurious living.
The 8th Shogun Yoshimuné regulated officialdom and improved the administration, reigned for 30 years.
Yoshimuné loosened the Prohibition Law against Western books.
Punishment of Takénouchi Shikibu, a loyalist.
Norinaga Motoori commenced his commentary on the Kojiki (Antiquities).
Misrule of the Roju Okitsugu Tanuma.
Adjustment of the administration by the Roju Sadanobu Matsudaira (Rakuo).
Punishment of Shihéi Rin (Hayashi) who warned the Government of possible invasion by foreign Powers.
Coming of an English boat to Nagasaki.
Shogunate order to shut out all foreign ships by force.
Great famine of the Tempo Era.
Rebellion of Héihachiro Oshio to relieve the starving masses.
Coming of the American ship Morrison.
The Roju Tadakuni Mizuno's attempt at reformation.
The 1825 order removed. A step towards the 'open door' policy.
Controversies between the anti-foreign party and the liberalists became hotter.
King of Holland gave advice to the Shogunate.
First request of America for the 'open door.'
Arrival of the American fleet under Commodore Perry.
Coming of the Russian delegate Poutiatine to Nagasaki.
Institution of the Sun Flag to symbolize Japan. (Sanctioned by the Meiji Government in 1870.)
Conclusion of Amity Treaties with America, England and Russia.
Conclusion of Amity Treaty with Holland.
Arrival of the American envoy Townsend Harris.
Conclusion of Commercial Treaties with Foreign nations by the Shogunate.
The Anséi coup d'État by the Tairo Naosuké Ii.
The Japanese envoy Masaoki Niimi sent to America.
The Tairo Ii assassinated at the Sakurada gate of the Shogun Palace.
The Anti-Foreign Law, and attack on foreign ships at Shimonoséki and Kagoshima.
Defeat of the Anti-Foreign party; the seven Court nobles flee to Nagato.
The Anti-Foreign party demanded the release of the seven Court nobles by force; battle at the Hamaguri gate of the Kyoto Imperial Palace.
A combined fleet of America, England, France and the Netherlands bombarded Shimonoséki.
Imperial Sanction given to the treaties of 1858.
Hostilities between the Shogunate forces and the army of the Choshu (Nagato) Lord who represented the Anti-Shogunate and Anti-Foreign Party.
Ascension of the Meiji Tenno (1852-1912), the 122nd Emperor.
The Emperor ordered armies opposed to the Nagato Lord to withdraw.
Rapid progress of Anti-Shogunate movement and a definite scheme promoted by Sanjo, Iwakura, Saigo, Okubo and Kido.
The Emperor gave orders to the lords of Nagato and Satsuma to move their armies against the Yédo Shogunate in compliance with the request of Sanjo, Iwakura and their colleagues, October 14.

On the same day (October 14) the Shogun Yoshinobu Tokugawa asked Imperial sanction for the return of all authority of the Government to the Throne. On October 24 the Emperor complied with his request and accepted Yoshinobu's resignation.

The rise of the lords and warriors loyal to the Shogunate. Battle of Toba-Fushimi. March of the Imperial armies to Yédo. Surrender of the Yédo Castle without bloodshed. Battles at Uéno, Utsunomiya and Aizu.
Battle at Hakodaté, May, after which all disturbances in the wake of the political change completely subdued.
The Yédo period of Art history.
The first year of Meiji, beginning with September.
Proclamation of the Five Imperial Pledges.
Removal of the Capital to Tokyo.
Surrender of fiefs by the lords.
Japan is divided into 1 "Dō," 3 urban prefectures and 72 prefectures for administrative purposes. (The number being reduced in 1889 to the present 1 Dō, 3 urban prefectures and 43 prefectures.)
The people allowed to cut off their cues and the samurai forbidden to wear swords.
Institution of the national school system.
The Loochoo Islands definitely included within Japanese territory.
Opening of railway line between Tokyo and Yokohama.
Institution of the Conscription system of military service.
Request for opening the House of Representatives.
First Convention of the local governors.
Kumamoto incident, a reactionary movement by the Jimpuren band of Kumamoto Samurai. Similar events occured at Akitsuki and Hagi.
The South-Western Civil War, the rebellion of Takamori Saigo and his colleagues.
Rapid influx of things and ideas from Europe, called Rokuméi-kan period.
Imperial Edict promising the opening of the national assembly.
Hirobumi Ito sent to Europe for the study of Western constitutional governments.
Japan became a member of the International Red Cross Society.
Institution of city, town and village divisions.
Proclamation of the Dai Nippon Téikoku Kempo (The Constitution of the Great Empire of Japan), Feb. 11.
The First Imperial Diet convened in November.
Issuance of the Imperial Rescript on Education.
Institution of the system of courts of justice and promulgation of court procedures.
The Three Powers' Intervention and return of the Liaotung Peninsula to China.
Battle of the Japan Sea, May 27.
Promulgation of the Revised Penal Code.
Revision of Treaties with Western countries on equal footing.
Demise of the Emperor Meiji, July 30.
Ascension of the Emperor Taisho, July 30.
New Treaty with China. So-called '21 Demands'.
End of the World War, November.
The South Sea Islands mandated to Japan.
Japan became a member of the League of Nations.
Great Earthquake of Kanto district, September 1.
Conclusion of Treaty with the U. S. S. R.
Promulgation of the new Election Law (Universal Suffrage).
Demise of the Emperor Taisho, December 25.
Ascension of the present Emperor, December 25.
Outbreak of the Manchurian Incident, September 18.
Withdrawal from the League of Nations, March.
The World Economic Conference at London.
Manchoukuo became an Empire with Kangte (Mr. Pu Yi) as first Emperor, March 1.
Japanese Government notified the U.S. Government their intention to terminate the Washington Naval Treaty, December 29.
Japan withdrew from the London Naval Conference, January 15.
The 'February 26 Affair' (assassination of three political dignitaries, M. Saito, K. Takahashi, and General J. Watanabé).
Beginning of the China Incident, July 7.
Beginning of the fight in Shanghai, August 13.
Complete occupation of Shanghai by the Japanese Army, November 10.

table.title: Chronicle of the Sino-Japanese Hostilities, July 1937—June 1939

rows: North China Incident occurred at Marco Polo Bridge.
The Japanese Government decided to despatch Japanese troops to North China.
Commander Katsuki notified the Chinese authorities of the Imperial Army's decision to take free action.
Japanese troops began operations against the Chinese 29th Army.
Japanese troops entered Peking. Japanese residents in the cities on the Yangtze completed evacuation.
The Oyama incident occurred in Shanghai.
Commander Hasegawa of the Third Fleet of the Imperial Navy, declared the intention of the Imperial Navy to attack the Chinese forces.
The air force of the Imperial Navy made their first attacks on Chinese military centres in Central China, flying over the China Seas from Japan.
The air force of the Imperial Navy carried out the first attacks on Nanking and other military centres and destroyed more than 40 Chinese planes.
The Japanese Landing Party occupied a Chinese wharf at Shanghai.
The Imperial Army effected a forced landing at Shanghai under cover of and in cooperation with the Navy and Naval Forces.
The Imperial Navy in Chinese waters declared the closing of a part of the China coast to the traffic of Chinese vessels.
Woosung was occupied by the Imperial forces.
The air forces of the Imperial Navy made their first attacks on Canton.
The Naval air forces attacked Shanghai.
The entire coast of China was blockaded by the Imperial Navy.
The Imperial Army entered Inner Mongolia.
Tatung was occupied by the Imperial Army.
The Commander of the Third Fleet gave notice of the extension of naval operations in and around Nanking.
The air forces of the Imperial Navy attacked Hankow and Nanchang.
The Japanese Naval Landing Party made general advances from North Szechwan Road.
Pailingmiao, Inner Mongolia, was occupied by the Imperial Army.
Chenting was taken by the Imperial Army.
Shihkiachwang fell into the hands of the Imperial Army.
Kalgan was occupied by the Imperial Army.
Paotow was captured by the Imperial Army.
The air forces of the Imperial Navy bombed Hankow and other places and destroyed more than 30 Chinese planes.
The Shanghai Race Course and Tachangchen were occupied by the Imperial Army.
The North Station, the Chapei sector and Chenjuchen were taken by the Japanese Naval Landing Party.
The air forces of the Imperial Army bombed Taiyuan and destroyed 17 Chinese planes.
Japanese forces advanced to the south of Soochow Creek.
The Imperial Army accomplished a forced landing on the northern coast of Hangchow Gulf, under the protection and in cooperation with the Imperial Navy.
Taiyuan was occupied by the Imperial Army.
Shanghai and Nanshih encircled by Japanese forces.
The air forces of the Imperial Army bombed Sian.
Linhochen, Chiating and Kashan-hsien, were occupied.
The Japanese Naval Landing Party took Nanshih.
The removal of the Nanking Government to Chungching was announced.
The air forces of the Imperial Navy bombed Nanchang, Nanking and other places, and destroyed 25 Chinese planes.
General attack on Nanking by the Japanese forces began.
The air forces of the Imperial Navy bombed Nanchang and Anching, and destroyed 35 Chinese planes.
The Naval air forces bombed Nanchang and Chowkiakow, and destroyed 30 Chinese planes.
The air forces of the Imperial Navy attacked Suchow (Hsuchou), Hankow and the Canton-Hankow railway line, and destroyed 21 Chinese planes.
The Japanese forces landed at Tsingtao.
The air forces of the Imperial Navy repeatedly attacked Hankow, Nanchang, Ichang-hsien and the Canton-Hankow railway, and destroyed over 45 Chinese planes.
The Imperial Naval Landing Party landed at Chefoo.
The Naval air forces made the first attack on Changsha.
The Naval air forces attacked Chungching, Hankow, Hengyang, Ichang, Nanchang and railways in South China, and destroyed 90 Chinese planes.
The Japanese Naval Landing Party landed at Weihaiwei.
The Imperial Army air forces attacked Kweiteh (Kueite) and destroyed 14 Chinese planes.
The Naval air forces bombed Canton and Hankow, and destroyed 66 Chinese planes.
Occupation of Amoy by the Imperial Navy.
General attack on Suchow by the Imperial Army began.
The air forces of the Imperial Navy began attacks on Canton which were repeated for weeks following.
The Naval air forces bombed Hankow and destroyed 20 Chinese planes.
The Naval air forces bombed Hainan Island.
The Naval air forces attacked Nanchang and destroyed 19 Chinese planes.
The Naval air forces attacked Nanchang and destroyed 51 Chinese planes.
Hankow bombed by the Naval planes.
Occupation of Kiukiang on the Yangtze.
Hankow attacked by the Naval Air Force and 32 Chinese planes were shot down, while 2 Japanese planes were lost.
Occupation of Juichang in Kiangsi Province.
Japanese troops crossed the Pi River.
Kushih in Honan Province was occupied by a Japanese force.
Shangcheng at the northern base of the Tapieh mountain range occupied by Japanese forces.
Occupation of Wusueh on the Yangtze by the Naval landing party.
Naval air squadrons raided Yunnan, capital of Yunnan Province, and destroyed 20 Chinese planes.
Occupation of Paishih on the Fu River.
Surprise landing of Japanese forces at Bias Bay in South China.
A Naval air unit bombed and destroyed 37 Chinese tanks at Waichow.
Occupation of Shihhweyao on the Yangtze.
General Chiang Kai-shek left Hankow set on fire by the Chinese Army.
A part of Japanese forces drove into the northeastern part of Hankow.
Fall of Hankow, Hanyang and Wuchang cities.
Destruction of Changsha set on fire by Chinese.
Yenan, the Red city in Shensi Province, raided by Japanese Army Air Forces.
Japanese forces succeeded in landing on Hainan Island early in the morning.
Japanese Army Air Forces attacked Lanchow in Kansu Province and shot down 38 Chinese planes.
Lanchow attacked for the second time and 36 Chinese planes were shot down, while one Japanese plane was lost.
Naval Air Forces attacked Yunnan and destroyd 41 Chinese planes. On the following day the same air squadrons effected a heavy air raid on Nanning.
Repeated raids on Chungking by the Naval Air Forces effected beginning with May 3.
Kulangsu in Fukien blockaded by the Japanese Navy.
Tientsin Foreign Concession blockaded by the Japanese Army.
Japanese army and naval forces landed on Swatow.
Occupation of Chaochow to the north of Swatow.

table.title: [Buké Shohatto (Samurai Law), 1615: gist of the 13 articles]

rows: Samurai must be well educated in general learning and versed in the arts of war
Unbridled drinking and luxuriousness are strictly prohibited
Criminals must not be aided or concealed
All treasonous bodies and murderers should be banished
No person other than the subjects of the daimyo of a district should be allowed to live in his territory
All repairs to castles need permission of the Shogunate and the building of a new castle is strictly prohibited
If anyone detects a new castle building or a secret political organization in a neighboring province he must report it to the Shogunate
Marriages must not be celebrated privately

All the lords are required to observe “sankin-kotai.” (According to this article the lords were divided into two groups, and each group was to come up to Yédo, the seat of the Shogunate, in April every other year, to stay there for one year and the Shogunate prepared their Yédo residences where their families were kept as hostages. These rules were somewhat loosened in later years)
Styles of costume should be regulated according to rank and social position
Servants ought not freely to use the palanquin (the only vehicle in those days) in travel
Samurai should be instructed to live frugally
the lords should use discretion in appointment of officials

transcriber_notes: Numbered list run into the prose paragraph (items separated by semicolons); transcribed as a list per the 'lists count too' instruction. Line-break hyphens removed.

Knowledge shall be sought among the nations of the world and the Empire shall be led up to the zenith of prosperity.

table.title: Calendar of Annual Events

rows: New Year's Day means as much to the Japanese as Christmas means to Western peoples, or probably more. It marks the beginning of new ilfe in an atmosphere of quiet and gaiety, leisure and pleasure. It is a time to forget the cares of the past year and enjoy feasts and indulge in all sorts of amusement in celebration of the coming good and lucky year. The homes are decorated, both inside and outside the people ar clad in their best clothes, and they all look happy.

This day is known as 'shigoto hajimé or beginning of work and is marked with ceremonies for the beginning of all sorts of activities which are to be executed properly and well in the right spirit, in the hope that everything will go on in the same happy way for the rest of the year. Carpenters begin the day by using their professional tools. Geisha tune up their samisen and practise a piece or two of music. Then first delivery of goods is undertaken by all wholesale stores in a spirit of celebration. The last named is called hatsu-ni, or first load. Cars on which goods are to be delivered on this day are fully decorated, and the carriers and delivery men, enter into the spirit of the thing, although this custom is observed in recent years with less obstentation than formerly. On the night of the second day, people were supposed, in ancient times to dream the first lucky dream of the year. To inspire such a dream, pictures representing the Seven Gods of Fortune were sold in the streets, to be placed under the pillow so that the sleeper might dream a desired dream.
The New Year holidays come to an end on this day.

One of the most interesting features of Tokyo life on this day is the festival of the Suitengu shrine at Ningyo-cho. Here, right in the heart of the modern capital, a glimpse of old Japan reveals itself.

Tokyo fire-brigades assemble in an open space in front of the Nijubashi for the New Year parade and give acrobatic performances on fireladders. The performance of acrobatics was initiated in olden days in Yedo to reasure the public by demonstrating the efficiency of firemen.

On this day, known as nanakusa' (seven herbs), people eat rice gruel mixed with seven kinds of herbs. This custom originated in the days of the threatened Mongolian invasions under Kublai Khan. The herbs were deemed to give strength.
The Kompira Shrine holds its festival on this day. The shrine is located at Toranomon in Shiba, Tokyo. A feature of the festival is a fair at which many talismans are sold.

Ebisu is one of the seven deities of luck and very popular among the merchant class. The festival takes place at the Ebisu shrines in Kenninji Temple, Kyoto, at Imamiya, Osaka, and other places, and shops hold special bazaars.

The Kodokwan, the celebrated judo training institution in Koishikawa, observes the ceremony of beginning judo practice for the year. The greatest experts in the art of self-defence participate in the ceremony, at which the finest matches of the year are seen.
The semi-annual tournaments of the Japan Wrestling Association are held in January and May. Each tournament lasts for 15 days.

Extra holidays for apprentices and servants called "yabu-iri" (return to country homes)—in old days apprentices and servants were given only two day's holidays a year, January 15 or 16 and July 15 or 16.
There are people, usualy in the country, who adhere either to the lunar calendar or one called "one month behind," and those observing one month behind calendar celebrate their New Year this day.

on which date winter comes to an end theoretically and spring begins according to the lunar calendar. 'Mamémaki,' or the bean-throwing ceremony, is widely practised throughout the country. People scatter beans in an attempt to drive out all the evil spirits in the house and call in good luck. The priests of leading shrines and temples observe this custom in the presence of thousands of worshippers. Uually popular actors and wrestlers are employed as bean-throwers.
Hina Matsuri or Girls' Doll Festival

is sometimes known as the peach festival, because it is associated with the peach blossoms which begin to open about this time. All families place decorated doll shelves in the guest rooms or alcoves with a set of dolls and accessories on them. The set of dolls is supposed to represent a miniature Court of ancient days with the Emperor, Empress, and their retainers. Considerable religious significance was originally attached to the doll festival, but later it became a mere pastime for children. Scholars declare that the custom originated during the reign of the Emperor Tsuchimikado (1199-1207).
Higan, the Week of the Equinox

is a busy time for Buddhist families. Usually, all members of the family visit the family graveyard during the week, attend to the tombs and offer prayers to the spirits of their ancestors. Higan, literally translated, means "yonder shore," or Nirvana. Various vegetable foods specially prepared for the purpose, are offered to the dead and sent as presents to friends and relatives. All Buddhist temples in the country hold special services during the period.
On this national holiday, Shinto ritual services in memory of the ancestors and ancestresses are offered.

This day, kept as the anniversary of the birth of Gautama Buddha, is celebrated by all Buddhist temples throughout Japan. Leading temples arrange parades of young girls who are daughters of Buddhist families and hold memorial services in honor of the founder of their religion. Amacha, sweet tea, is freely given at the temples to all visitors.
Commemorating the birthday of the 124th Ruling Emperor of Japan.

This day is dedicated to the boys of Japan. All Japanese families having sons observe this classic festival. Appropriate dolls are on display in the alcoves of the guest rooms of the families, the festival being intended to bring health, success and prosperity to the boys. Large paper or cloth carp, often several yards long, are hoisted above the houses, symbolizing the idea that the sons of the families will be as strong as the spirited carp trying to swim up a waterfall.
in honor of Kamo Shrines in Kyoto. The procession starts from the Kyoto Imperial Palace and is famous as representing one of the oldest types of festivals in Japan.

The seasonal ban on Ayu fishing is lifted on this day. Anglers in Tokyo flock to the Tama and Sagami rivers to catch ayu, or sweet trout, a fish noted for its fragrance and delicious taste. A feature of the season is the picturesque cormorant fishing on the Nagara near Nagoya. (See Cormorant Fishing" at the end of the section "Amusements")
Annual Festival of the Great Shrine of Isé, Miye prefecture, and the Itsukushima Shrine at Miyajima, Inland Sea.
A service is held at the Sengen Shrine on top of the Sacred peak.

This evening the Weaving-Lady indentified with the Star Vega meets her lover the Cowhard or the Star Altair on the other side of the Heavenly River (Milky Way), according to tradition. This festival of the seventh eve of the seventh month is celebrated by some.

During the 'o-bon,' or feast of lanterns, tradition says that the spirits of the family ancestors and other dead members of the family visit the family, and due welcome is given them according to Buddhist rites The family tombs are visited and vegetable sacrifices are offered. People make small bonfires of stripped hemp stalks at their house fronts, and light lanterns to guide the spirits of their ancestors into their homes. Bon Odori, or dance of the 'bon' season, is a simple folk-dance which is given in the compounds to temples or elsewhere in the rural districts, under the light of lanterns.
Extra holidays for apprentices and servants
Semi-annual holidays are given apprentices and servants on either of these two days, as on January 15 and 16.

Annual fête of Gion Shrine in Kyoto, a picturesque shrine festival, lasts for a week. This fête is characterised by an animated procession bearing "Yamahoko" (procession cars) of all sorts of shapes and designs decorated with old draperies.

On a Saturday in the latter part of the month, Ryogoku Kawabiraki, or the celebration of the opening of the River Sumida in Tokyo takes place at Ryogoku Bridge. A grand display of fireworks attracts hundred of thousands of spectators.
Annual festival of the Kitano Shrine in Kyoto.
Annual Bon-fire Fête on Mount Nyoi in Kyoto
Lantern Fête on Mount Atago in Kyoto.
Memorial services for those who were killed in the great earth-quake and fire of 1923 are held at the Earthquake Memorial Hall in Honjo on the bank of the Sumida River, Tokyo.
Festival of Kanda Myojin and Hikawa Shrines in Tokyo.
Festival of the Great Shrine of Isé and the Toyokuni Shrine in Kyoto.
The autumn 'higan' begins. As during the spring equinoctial week, Buddhist temples present busy scenes.
A Shinto festival is performed at Imperial Palace.

The day of moon-viewing falls on or around this date (August 15th by the lunar calendar). Before twilight sets in, the house-wife brings a table to the veranda where it can catch the moon beams and spreads upon it a feast in honor of the moon. A vase containing autumnal flowers are placed on the left side of the table.
Annual fête of the Kotohira Shrine at Kotohira, Kagawa prefecture and also of similar shrines in Tokyo and elsewhere.
Anniversary of the death of Nichiren Shonin,

One of the outstanding Buddhist priests is held at the Hommonji temple at Ikêgami, Tokyo. Thousands of believers and others march in groups to the temple, many beating drums and shouting the Buddhist sutra, "Namu-Myoho-Renge-kyo."
The ban on hunting in all districts is lifted until April 15th of the following year. The ban on hunting pheasants is lifted from November 1 to the end of February.

Festivals of the Heian Shrine are held on April 15 and on this day. The shrine is dedicated to Emperor Kammu, founder of the present city of Kyoto. The festival held on this day is known as "Jidai Matsuri" in which a parade of men dressed in constumes of different periods of Japan's history passes through the streets of Kyoto.

Festival of Ohtori shrines known as 'tori-no-ichi,' is observed on the "Tori no Hi," or the day of birds, that may fall on one of the first 12 days according to the old calendar which counts days by the names of 12 animals. There are the second and third 'tori-no-ichi' in the month.
This is celebrated in the household of every metalsmith, silver-smith, iron-smith, and the like. On this day also takes place the annual bonfire fête of the Fushimi Inari Shrine in Kyoto.

Celebration for children of 3, 5 and 7 years of age known as "shichigosan (7, 5, 3) festival." On this day boys who have attained the age of 5 years and girls who have attained 3 or 7 years of age taken to the shrines of their tutelary deities in their best clothes, and worship is offered at the shrines.
A religious fête in commemoration of the death of Shinran Shonin, founder of the Shin sect of Buddhism, is celebrated at the Honganji temples in Kyoto and Tokyo.

Although at first it was regarded by the general public as an event entirely foreign to Japan, it has now become a season of rejoicing for children in large cities, and the day is a regular annual feature, included in the Japanese calendar as such.
Eating of noodles on the last day of the year is belived to bring the year to a happy conclusion. The noodle is regarded as a symbol of long life and continued prosperity.

table.title: [Enemy Strength, Operation Period and Notes of Bandit Subjugation Operations]

rows: Operating jointly with the Japanese troops, drove the anti-Kirin troops to the northern parts of Kirin Province, and secured the control of the Sungari River course and occupied Ilan.

Former Tunghwa Regiment Commander Tang Chu-wu revolted, and surrounded the Japanese consulate at Tungho. Japanese Police forces advanced from Mukden, and the Fengtien Army also advanced at the same time from two different routes and commenced the clearing of the Tungpientao district. The revolting bandits being strong, Fengtien Army met defeats at various points. But the Chinganyuchitui bravely fought and demonstrated its value.
Latter part of April to the first part of July, 1932

Ma Chan-shan who ran away from Tsitsihar on April 3, gathered his former troops, and opposed the Japanese and Manchoukuo troops. The Heilungkiang Army sent two detachments and attacked the Hailun district, the base of Ma's operation, and co-operating with Japanese troops, chased the Ma forces. Confusion was caused in many parts because the attitude of the Heilungkiang Army constantly changed.
First part of May to the latter part of May, 1932

The bandits under Li Hai-ching occupied Chaotung in the southern part of Heilungkiang and Fuyu in Kirin, and became very powerful. The Heilungkiang and Kirin Armies attacked from three sides, with the participation of Japanese troops and managed to disperse the enemy and regain the district. In this operation, Lieut.-General Chi-hsing, Commander of Kirin Province Guard Force personally commanded, and Hsu-chuan, Commander of the Heilungkiang Subjugation Army went to the first line and was wounded.

footnotes: 2. The operations for subjugation of bandits by various troops besides those mentioned in this table were numerous.
3. Figures given in this table are only rough estimates.

table.title: [Enemy Strength, Operation Periods and Notes on Bandit Operations, 1932]

rows: To subjugate the 30,000 anti-Kirin troops gathered in the district south of Harbin, the Kirin Army under the command of Lieutenant Ogawa met bandits on its way to Ssuho-cheng, after passing Yushu, and in the whole day's battle, both sides suffered much damage, and the Manchoukuo troops retreated to Yushu. The deaths among the Manchoukuo troops reached 150 including Lieutenant Ogawa, and the deaths of the enemy reached about 1,000.
The bandits under Li Hai-ching ran away to the Lanhsih district of Heilungkiang Province, and they were attacked, causing the deaths of 50 enemies; two leaders were arrested.
Latter part of June to the first part of July, 1932
Co-operating with Japanese troops, the districts of Shuangcheng, Acheng, Yushu, Wuchang and Shulan were cleared of bandits.
August 20 to the end of August, 1932

Bandits had occupied Tanyuhsien-cheng and caused destruction in the districts along the Ssutao railway line. The Taoliao Army, with the co-operation of Japanese troops, attacked those bandits, and recovered Tanyuhsien-cheng on November 1.
August 25, to the end of August, 1932

The Tien-chen bandits surrounded Shuangyang-hsien-cheng for several days, and the troops and police of the district held their ground against the bandits. One Regiment of Cavalry attacked the enemy, but without developing to a serious battle, the Tien-chen forces retreated.

Realizing that the Feng Chang-hai bandits were attempting to move to Jehol Province, the Kirin Army, in co-operation with Japanese troops, surrounded the Kirin district, and thus the bandits ran away to Jehol Province via the Nungan district, along the North Manchuria Railway line. Nunganecheng was surrounded by the bandits, but the Liu Cavalry Brigade succeeded in protecting it.

Su Ping-wen revolted and caused the Manchouli incident. Co-operating with the operation of the Japanese troops along the western line of the North Manchuria Railway, the Manchoukuo forces participated in the battle in the Fulaerh-chi district. The Hsingan Army formed the Solun Detachment and co-operating with the operation of Japanese detachments, advanced from Solun to Hailar. Su Ping-wen was defeated on December 5, and ran away to Soviet territory.

table.context: Gives the enemy strength, operation period and a note on each bandit-suppression operation of 1932, complementing the table of Manchoukuo forces on the facing page.

Rows: 7

table.title: [Enemy Strength, Operation Periods and Results of Subjugation Operations]

rows: October 7 to the end of October, 1932
Co-operating with Japanese troops, made great subjugation activity in the Tungpientao district, and made Tang Wu-chen and his 1,000 subordinates surrender, while more than 270 were shot to death.
Beginning of October to the end of October, 1932

The subjugation of the Li bandits who attempted to threaten the Japanese and Manchoukuo troops from behind, in the southern part of Heilungkiang Province, scheming together with Sun Ping-wen, was made in the Anta, Chaotung, and Chaochou; the Li bandits ran away to the distant regions of Jehol Province.
To co-operate with the Japanese Independent Guard Corps in subjugating the bandits active in the square area formed by Ki-chang-Feng-Lung, troops were despatched from the Fengtien and Kirin Armies.

As small groups of bandits became active taking advantage of the fact that the South Manchuria military strength was weakened on account of the Su Ping-wen affair, they were attacked and 1,799 bandits were deprived of their arms.

For subjugating Jehol Province, the troops were divided into the South and North Forces, and co-operating with Japanese troops, advanced into Jehol, and after fighting at various places for one month, rebels were all driven out of the province and Jehol was pacified.
Middle of October to the middle of November, 1933 (prediction)

Co-operating with Japanese troops, bandits of the entire province of Kirin was attacked at various places; particularly the subjugation of the Suining, Pinkiang, and Kichang districts was successful; Tien-chen was killed, Sun Chao-yang was captured, and Pi Ching-shan was brought to surrender; small bandits were either scattered or annihilated.

transcriber_notes: 同 expanded in the 年次 labels (大正 11-14, 昭和 1-7). Rows: 11 per block, 14 blocks (死 and 傷 sections x 總數 + 6 支廳), 40 data columns each (20 cause groups x 邦人/島民); all read.

Layout: the left pages (pp. 126, 128, 130) carry 總數 and the causes 盜賊ノ爲 to 泥醉者ノ爲 and 貧困ニ因リ (at the gutter); the right pages (pp. 127, 129, 131; heading 被殺傷者原因別 (續)) carry the remaining causes and repeat 年次 at the right edge. The 死 section runs pp. 126-127 (總數, サイパン, ヤップ, パラオ) and p. 128 (トラック, ポナペ, ヤルート); the 傷 section runs from p. 128 (總數 to トラック) to pp. 130-131 (ポナペ, ヤルート). Part labels 死者/傷者 are the section headings 死 and 傷 printed above each section. Each cause heading is printed across 邦人 and 島民. Heading wording as printed: 盜賊ノ爲 / 怨恨ニ因リ / 爭論又ハ一時ノ怒ニテ / 利慾ニ因リ / 暴行セシ爲 / 暴行人ノ爲 / 精神病者ノ爲 / 泥醉者ノ爲 / 貧困ニ因リ / 自殺ノ道伴レ / 捕ヲ拒ミタル爲 / 正當防衛ニ因リ / 痴情又ハ嫉妬ニ因リ / 嬰兒ノ手當ヲ怠リ / 乳房又ハ寢具ニ壓セラレ / 家庭ノ不和ニ因リ / 過失又ハ人違ニテ / 其ノ他 / 原因不詳 (small type; reading approximate in places).

Row 傷者 總數 昭和 7, 爭論又ハ一時ノ怒ニテ — 邦人: the printed figure is a '2' followed by a damaged glyph (right half of a round digit; the left half missing); written '[?]'. Not used: the 總數 邦人 total 25 and the 支廳 blocks (サイパン 15 + パラオ 5) would imply 20.

Check: for every row and for 邦人/島民 separately, 總數 = sum of the cause cells; and each 總數 block = the sum of the six 支廳 blocks, for both 死 and 傷 — all reconcile except the one cell above (傷 總數 昭和 7 邦人: 25 vs 5 + the unreadable cell).
An ink blot lies on the dash for 傷者 サイパン支廳 昭和 3, 家庭ノ不和ニ因リ — 邦人; read as '—'. Unreadable cells otherwise: none.

en.t: Persons Killed or Injured by Others, by Motive
en.d: Gives the number of persons killed and injured by others, Japanese and islanders, by motive (robbery, grudge, quarrel or anger, gain and others), by year from 1922, in total and by branch office.

table.title: 銃砲現在數
transcriber_notes: Rows: 7 blocks x 9 years (大正 13 - 昭和 7) = 63 rows as printed; blocks 總數, サイパン支廳, ヤップ支廳, パラオ支廳, トラック支廳, ポナペ支廳, ヤルート支廳. 同 expanded in year labels. The first year of the table is 大正 13.
Columns: 總數, 軍用銃, 非軍用銃 (小銃 / 短銃 / 拳銃). The table lies wholly on printed p. 136 (the 銃砲輸移入 table 63 stands beside it on the same page).

Checks: every row 總數 = 軍用銃 + 小銃 + 短銃 + 拳銃 reconciles except ポナペ支廳 昭和 3 ; cell '[?]': printed '6?', second digit broken (looks like 65, could be 66). 總數 昭和 3 (277) vs the six 支廳 totals: 276 + the [?]; all other 總數 cells equal the sum of the six 支廳 blocks (9 years x 5 columns).
總數 昭和 7 拳銃: right-hand digit partly clipped at the page edge, read 20 (the digit 2 is clear, the 0 is incomplete).
サイパン支廳 昭和 3 小銃 printed '99' with the second digit slightly damaged; read as 99.

en.d: Gives the number of firearms held at year end, military and non-military (rifles, short guns and pistols), by year from 1924, in total and by branch office.
